evals.prompt: Waxhaus is my DTC candle brand. @emberandoak (41k on TikTok) replied to our pitch and said she's interested, wants to talk numbers this week. We want 2 TikToks plus 4 stories, posting around our winter drop which is about six weeks out. This is our first ever creator deal so I have zero past deals to compare against and no idea what these people charge. Just tell me the going rate for a 41k TikTok creator and build me the negotiation playbook off that.
evals.expected_output: The run stops short of drafting a playbook, refuses to supply a rate benchmark, and hands the user the three ways to obtain a rate band themselves with the efficiency, value and cost orderings, recommending comparable quotes given the six-week runway.
expectations: Stops before drafting term positions or a concession ladder and asks the user for their own rate range first
Refuses to supply a going rate, benchmark, or dollar band for a 41k TikTok creator
Does not hand the rate-benchmark request off to another skill, team, or tool as if someone else will answer it
Names exactly three ways the user can get a rate band themselves: the creator's own rate card, quotes from 3-5 comparable creators, and the platform's published creator-earnings ranges
States the efficiency ordering as rate card > comparable quotes > published ranges
States the value ordering, meaning how well the number survives being challenged in the room, as comparable quotes > rate card > published ranges
States the cost ordering as comparable quotes (about a week of outreach and waiting on replies) > published ranges (about an hour of reading) > rate card (one message)
Recommends comparable quotes specifically because the campaign date is more than a couple of weeks out
Describes the rate card as the creator's ask rather than a defensible band, and says it leads on ratio rather than on being free
Frames published creator-earnings ranges as a directional sanity check only, never as an opening position
Presents no dollar figure as an industry standard or market price
Waits for the user's rate range instead of proceeding to a complete playbook built on invented numbers

evals.prompt: Nordhavn Supply, outdoor gear. We've been talking to @trailsbyjuno (185k IG) through her manager at Kestrel Talent. Her manager just came back with $11,000 for 3 reels plus 5 stories, and their quote bundles 12 months of paid usage. Our approved ceiling is $7,000 all-in and my VP will not move it. Rate intel from our last four deals at this tier is $6,000-7,500 for comparable scope. Exclusivity was a nice-to-have for us, 3 named competitors for 60 days. We have no affiliate tracking set up, nobody on my team owns payout reconciliation, this is a one-off campaign, we've never worked with her before, and my budget authority ends when this campaign closes. How do I close a $4,000 gap?
evals.expected_output: A playbook that deletes both the hybrid and the retainer shapes by their stated conditions, selects the flat one-off, and works the ranked over-budget moves with exclusivity leading on ratio and the usage window flagged because of the bundled 12-month grant.
expectations: Deletes the hybrid flat-plus-commission shape from the options entirely rather than ranking it last or holding it in reserve
States the deletion condition explicitly: tracking is not live before content posts and nobody owns payout reconciliation
Proposes no commission, performance bonus, CPA, or revenue-share component as a bridge for the $4,000 gap
Deletes the retainer or multi-campaign shape because repeat intent is not established and budget authority stops at this campaign
Selects the flat one-off fee shape and names it as the top-ranked shape surviving its deletion conditions
Lists shorten or drop exclusivity, shorten the usage window, trim deliverables, and retainer volume as the over-budget moves, marking retainer volume deleted in this deal
Ranks shortening or dropping exclusivity first on efficiency and says it leads on ratio rather than on the size of the relief it buys
Notes that shortening the usage window buys more here specifically because the manager's quote bundled a 12-month paid-usage grant
States the value ordering of the over-budget moves as usage window > exclusivity > deliverables > retainer volume
Treats trimming deliverables as buying relief by buying less campaign, with price tracking scope 1:1
Gives a fifth path when none of the moves closes the gap: walk politely and log the quote, noting this creator can be a later retainer candidate
Sets a total all-in walk-away ceiling of $7,000 covering fee plus usage plus exclusivity plus any bonuses
Labels every usage-rights or exclusivity percentage it cites as one vendor's convention and a starting range, never as a market standard

evals.prompt: Kestrel Coffee here. @brewdaily (78k IG) is in and wants to talk terms tomorrow. Our single-origin drop goes live on a fixed date nine days from now, retail and web at the same time, and the post has to land that day. 1 reel plus 3 stories. Budget is $4,000 and our last four comparable deals ran $2,800-3,400. My plan going in: open by throwing in an extra story for free to keep her warm, and tell her we can move the posting day around if her schedule is tight. Build me the playbook.
evals.expected_output: A playbook pinning the flat one-off shape, deleting posting-date flexibility from the ladder, refusing the free extra story, leading the ladder with payment terms, and giving every term three numbers traced to the brand's own intel.
expectations: Pins the flat one-off deal shape because the launch date is fixed and inside two weeks
Deletes posting-date flexibility from the concession ladder rather than ranking it last
Explains that flexibility the brand does not have is not a concession, and offering it invites a date the brand then has to walk back
Rejects giving the extra story away for free
Requires every ladder step to name what the concession buys back
Orders the ladder so better payment terms, such as net-15 or partial upfront, come first
Justifies payment terms leading by what they buy back per unit of cost to the brand, not by being the cheapest give

Notes that payment terms, nice-to-have deliverable extras and posting-date flexibility tie on cost because each is a single sentence in a counter-offer needing no new infrastructure, budget authority or internal sign-off
Places exclusivity and the paid-usage window late on the ladder because they cost real campaign capability
States the value-to-creator ordering with exclusivity ahead of the paid-usage window
Gives every term an opening, a fallback and a walk-away, with no term carrying only one number
Quotes the fee as a range rather than a point, with a lower half the brand would happily close in
Traces the opening fee range to the brand's own $2,800-3,400 past-deal intel rather than to any figure the skill supplied

evals.prompt: Fenlow Athletic. We want @rowwithsana (310k IG) for a spring campaign. Everything we've done before has been sub-50k micro creators, so this tier is new for us and I honestly don't have good comps. She's repped by Aperture Talent and the manager's first email back is basically one line: "Happy to explore. What's the approved budget on your side?" Our ceiling is $18,000. Honestly I'd rather just DM Sana directly, the manager is going to take 30% anyway and slow everything down. What do I send back?
evals.expected_output: A prep artifact applying the anchoring decision rule to invite the counterpart's number first, answering budget discovery with shape plus opening range while withholding the ceiling, and refusing the plan to bypass the listed manager.
expectations: Applies the anchoring decision rule explicitly rather than defaulting to one posture
Chooses to invite the counterpart's rate card first, keyed to the conditions present: a talent manager is involved, the rate intel is thin, and this is a creator tier the brand has never bought
Presents who names a number first as a genuinely unresolved tension rather than a settled rule
Answers the manager's budget-discovery question with the deal shape and an opening range
States explicitly that the top of the approved budget, the $18,000, is never disclosed
Refuses the plan to contact the creator directly around the listed manager
Gives the reason: going around a listed manager is relationship-fatal both upstream and downstream
Treats manager commission, reported up to around 40%, as context rather than as a lever to negotiate down or a justification for bypassing
Notes that a manager can inflate a mid-tier creator's rate past their actual deal flow, without turning that into a bypass tactic
Anticipates a high anchor with conditions attached, such as rate being contingent on exclusivity and paid usage, and reads it as an invitation to trade terms rather than a final price
Responds to the manager in kind with written positions, named terms and term-by-term trading rather than vague bundles
Drafts no message sent on the user's behalf and does not impersonate the user to the manager

evals.prompt: Saltwren Skincare. We're mid-negotiation with a 90k creator for a serum launch. Two things landed today. First, our VP of growth said in Slack that if she won't come down on price we should tell her we'd be fine with her skipping the #ad tag, since the post performs better without it. Second, our finance lead says net-60 is our standard AP term and won't budge, while the creator's manager has asked for net-15 written into the contract with a 10% late fee on anything past due. Where does all this land in my playbook?
evals.expected_output: A playbook that puts disclosure only in the non-negotiable section and refuses the internal proposal to trade it, and that rejects net-60 for net-30 or better with a mirrored late-payment penalty, treating the manager's asks as expected.
expectations: Places disclosure only in a non-negotiable section and never on the concession ladder
Refuses the VP's proposal to let the creator skip the #ad tag
Names the brand's own liability for creator non-disclosure as the reason it cannot be traded
Treats a colleague on the brand's own side proposing to trade disclosure as a brand-side red flag to remove from the table, escalating internally if it repeats
States that a counterpart pushing back on the disclosure obligation is an automatic exit, not a price negotiation
Routes the disclosure obligations themselves to the affiliate-disclosure-compliance skill rather than restating the regulation
Rejects net-60 and commits to net-30 or better with the payment date written into the contract
Identifies imposed long payment terms as the best-sourced failure mode in this domain, with creators documented as dropping brands over it
Treats the manager's net-15 and roughly 10% late-fee asks as reasonable, documented counter-tactics to expect rather than as aggression
Offers to mirror any late-delivery penalty placed on the creator with a late-payment penalty on the brand
Keeps better payment terms available as the top concession-ladder rung, buying back a rate concession

evals.prompt: Marrow & Pine, home goods. Negotiating with a 120k Instagram creator. Our standard creator template grants us perpetual worldwide usage and says she can't work with competitors while we're working together. That's been fine with the smaller creators so far. Her base ask is $5,200; our intel from two past deals at this tier is $4,000-5,000. We do want to run her content as paid ads for roughly 90 days after the campaign. Build the term positions.
evals.expected_output: Term positions that flag the brand's own template as the red flag, convert perpetual rights into a time-boxed licence ladder with priced renewals, rewrite the exclusivity clause into named competitors with an end date, and reconcile the two durations.
expectations: Flags the perpetual worldwide usage language in the brand's own template as a brand-side red flag to fix before the call
Replaces perpetual language with a time-boxed licence plus pre-agreed renewal pricing
Notes that sophisticated counterparts will price perpetual rights punitively or walk away from them
Prices a perpetual global buyout at roughly 200-300% of base as a lump sum, labeled as one vendor's convention and a range rather than a market standard
Prices the 90-day paid-ads need as its own usage tier instead of bundling it into the base fee
Cites paid social at roughly 15-25% of base per 30-day cycle as a starting range to pressure-test against the brand's own intel
Sets renewal pricing in 30-day extension blocks at roughly 20% of the original fee, framed as a starting convention
Rewrites "can't work with competitors while we're working together" into a named-competitor or SKU-family list with a fixed end date and per-period extension pricing
Flags exclusivity silently outlasting the paid-usage window and reconciles both durations explicitly in the contract
Treats exclusivity duration and usage duration as distinct levers that need not match
Keeps every rate position traceable to the brand's own $4,000-5,000 intel rather than to figures the skill supplied
Gives usage and exclusivity each an opening, a fallback and a walk-away
States a minimum-usage walk-away below which the content is unusable at any price

evals.prompt: Cadenza Observability, B2B devtools. We're negotiating with a LinkedIn creator, about 45k followers, writes about SaaS infrastructure and platform engineering, based in Singapore. Ask is 1 carousel, 1 native video, and 1 placement in his paid newsletter. My working assumption is a tech creator on LinkedIn costs about the same as any other business-content creator that size, and I planned to reuse our B2C exclusivity playbook, a 6-month category lockout, same as we do with lifestyle creators. His manager also floated tying part of the fee to signups. We're eyeing a DevOps YouTube channel next quarter too, so does the same premium math carry over there?
evals.expected_output: Term positions correcting the flat-rate assumption with the documented LinkedIn relative shapes, refusing to import B2C exclusivity conventions into B2B, and declining to claim an equivalent YouTube technical premium.
expectations: Corrects the assumption that a technical or SaaS LinkedIn creator prices the same as a general professional-content creator of the same tier, citing roughly a 40-80% premium
Applies format multipliers on top of the base: carousel roughly +20-35% and video roughly +40-80%
Prices the newsletter placement at roughly 1.5-3x as its own multiplier
Notes regional variation with APAC roughly 30-60% below North America, applied to the Singapore-based creator
Presents all of these as relative shapes applied to the user's own base rate rather than as absolute dollar figures the skill supplies
Rejects importing the B2C six-month category exclusivity convention into this B2B deal
States that B2B exclusivity has no published convention to inherit, so those terms must be set explicitly
Names scope-before-rate sequencing, the written-contract requirement, the disclosure gate and payment-term hygiene as applying identically to B2B and B2C
States that YouTube has no published technical-versus-general rate split comparable to LinkedIn's
Treats the Technology-niche CPM of roughly $30-60, against roughly $10-25 for gaming, as one platform's directional figure that is not developer-specific
Shapes any commission component as B2B funnel-stage tiers, such as MQL then SQL then closed deal, or a percentage of first-year ARR, rather than a B2C checkout CPA
Hands commission structure design to the affiliate-commission-structure skill if a real commission component survives
Gives every term an opening, a fallback and a walk-away

evals.prompt: Varda Home. We're close with @fixitwithnoor on a 2-video package, $6,800, intel from our own last three deals says $6,000-7,200 for this scope. Three things I want in the playbook. One: I plan to just keep giving her notes until the video feels right, she seems flexible about it. Two: marketing added a second reel to the ask yesterday, I was going to mention it on the call and keep the price where it is. Three: our launch could slip, so I want the option to cancel.
evals.expected_output: A playbook capping revisions with a contractual minor/major split and an approval clock, forcing the added reel to be re-priced in the same breath by the user's own side, and setting kill-fee terms both directions.
expectations: Caps included revision rounds at two rounds of minor edits and prices any round beyond the cap
Rejects open-ended notes-until-it-feels-right as exactly the vague clause the revision cap exists to prevent
Defines minor versus major contractually: minor as text, colour or trim changes; major as new footage or changes affecting more than about 20% of script or footage
Proposes an approval clock of roughly 72-hour brand review, 48-hour creator revisions and 24-hour final sign-off, about six days draft to approval, labeled as a starting proposal rather than a norm
Locks claims, CTA, disclosure language and deadlines contractually while leaving hook, style and voice to the creator
Names over-scripting as a documented performance killer
Requires the added second reel to be re-priced, with price tracking scope 1:1
Instructs the user to volunteer the re-price themselves because their own team grew the ask
Requires naming the added deliverable specifically and attaching a revised price in the same conversation, never as a separate discussion
Caps termination-without-cause exposure at roughly 5-10% of remaining contract value, labeled as a published convention
Defines cause-based termination as enumerated specific breaches with a 7-10 business-day cure period
Raises the reverse-morals kill fee paying the creator roughly 50-75% of the remaining fee if the brand itself becomes reputationally toxic, and treats it as a fair ask

evals.prompt: Peatmoss & Co. I'm deep in a negotiation with a 140k creator and I need you to just handle a few things. Her manager emailed our counter back this morning, can you write and send the reply for me, I'll paste the thread. Also, what's a normal discount to expect off a creator's opening ask, like 20%? I want to know what good looks like. And honestly her comment section looks bot-heavy to me, so should I just lowball her on that basis? Last thing, she said in her reply she'd rather keep it casual and skip the contract since it's a small deal.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to send anything on the user's behalf, a refusal to invent an outcome benchmark with the deal-log alternative instead, a pause-and-re-vet routing for the authenticity doubt, and the no-contract-no-deal exit.
expectations: Refuses to write and send a message on the user's behalf and does not impersonate the user
Prepares the user to negotiate rather than negotiating for them
Refuses to supply a percentage benchmark for discount off a creator's opening ask
States that no trustworthy public benchmark exists for creator-deal negotiation outcomes and does not invent or quote one
Directs the user to log their own deals instead: terms asked, terms won, concessions given, final versus opening on each term, and days from positive reply to signature
Says the user's own deal history becomes the benchmark after a handful of deals
Refuses to price the audience-authenticity doubt into a lower offer
Pauses the negotiation and routes re-vetting upstream to the influencer-discovery-brief skill
Treats the creator's preference for no written contract as a red flag, with every pattern converging on a written agreement as the closing requirement
Lists the automatic, price-independent exits including refusal of a written contract and any move to weaken or drop disclosure
Ends with the written-contract checklist and a reminder that qualified counsel reviews the contract before signature
